title: WILDTRACE: Benchmarking Natural Evidence Trails in Long-Context Reasoning
hook: Most long-context tests plant a fake 'needle' in a haystack. Real evidence doesn't look like that — passing needle tests may not mean a model can truly reason over a document.
key_points: 481 tasks built over 214 real long documents — incident reports, literary narratives — not synthetic needle-in-haystack setups.
Planted/needle evidence differs from real evidence in distribution and placement, so needle tests may not measure real reasoning.
Defines seven 'source-internal evidence geometries,' from Pearl's causal hierarchy, for how evidence naturally connects in a document.
Source-first pipeline: mines candidate evidence trails from a document's structure, then validates clue necessity and groundedness.
From a Qwen/Alibaba team; frames dispersed evidence integration as the next challenge for long-context research.
content_html: Real analytical reading over long documents means connecting evidence the document itself scatters naturally — the operating condition and design flaw behind an incident may sit sections apart; a character's true motive may only surface scenes later. Most long-context benchmarks sidestep this by planting facts or reverse-engineering multi-hop chains, which may differ from how evidence actually appears in real text.
extra_html: WildTrace, from a Qwen/Alibaba team including Fei Huang and Dayiheng Liu, instead builds 481 tasks over 214 naturally occurring long-form sources — technical incident reports and lesser-known literary narratives — where every evidence trail arises from the document's own causal, temporal, and narrative logic. Drawing on Pearl's causal hierarchy and prior multi-hop reasoning typologies, the authors define seven "source-internal evidence geometries" that characterize how real evidence naturally connects. Construction is source-first: candidate trails are mined from a document's existing structure before questions are even written, then validated for clue necessity, answer groundedness, rubric fidelity, contamination resistance, and answerability. The takeaway is a warning as much as a benchmark — the gap between accessing information and reasoning over evidence as it naturally appears may be the real test long-context research still needs to pass. See arxiv.org/abs/2607.09328.

related.title: Why Long-Context Speed Comes Down to Prefill and KV Heads
related.hook: Everyone benchmarks token-generation speed. A community test of 13 models at 65K-128K context found that's the wrong number — prefill dominates, and KV head count beats parameter count.

related.title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory
related.hook: Agent memory sounds purely good — until retrieved memories start pushing an agent to agree with the user over the facts. MemSyco-Bench is built specifically to catch that failure.

flashcards.prompt: What methodological problem does WildTrace raise about typical long-context benchmarks?
flashcards.back_html: Needle-in-a-haystack-style planted facts differ from real evidence in distribution, placement, and register — so passing them may not reflect genuine long-context reasoning.

flashcards.prompt: What does WildTrace use as its evidence source, instead of planted facts?

choices.text: 481 tasks built from 214 naturally occurring long documents like incident reports and literary narratives
Synthetic passages generated by an LLM specifically for each question
Short texts with reverse-engineered multi-hop chains inserted

flashcards.explanation_html: WildTrace mines evidence trails already present in real documents' own causal, temporal, and narrative structure, rather than planting them.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'source-internal evidence geometry' in WildTrace?
flashcards.back_html: One of seven relational patterns, drawn from Pearl's causal hierarchy and multi-hop reasoning work, describing how naturally dispersed evidence connects within a document.

flashcards.prompt: How does WildTrace's construction pipeline avoid inserting artificial evidence?

choices.text: It mines candidate evidence trails from a document's existing structure before writing questions
It asks annotators to invent facts and insert them into the source text
It only uses questions answerable from a single sentence

flashcards.explanation_html: A source-first pipeline extracts trails already present in the document, then validates each item for clue necessity, groundedness, and contamination resistance.
